expected_evidence: Geological: elevated platinum (and other platinum-group element) concentrations in a thin layer within Greenland ice cores dated to ~12,900 years BP (the Younger Dryas onset boundary)
Geological: correlated platinum/iridium anomaly in terrestrial sediment cores and paleosols at the Younger Dryas boundary (YDB) layer across multiple continents
Geological: presence of impact-diagnostic markers in the same stratigraphic layer — nanodiamonds, magnetic and glassy microspherules, melt-glass, high-temperature soot/charcoal ('black mat')
Geological: a shocked-quartz or crater signature (e.g., a candidate impact structure such as the proposed Hiawatha crater under the Greenland ice) with age constraints matching -10950
Astronomical: reconstructable orbital/dynamical evidence of a fragmented comet or asteroid stream intersecting Earth at this date (indirect, model-based)
Genetic/faunal: megafaunal extinction and population bottleneck signatures in North American/Eurasian species dated to the same interval
Material/archaeological: disruption or discontinuity in Clovis-era (or contemporaneous) archaeological sites in the Americas coincident with the layer
Model-prior: consistency with the broader Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis literature (Firestone et al., Petaev et al., Kennett et al.), noting this remains scientifically contested
response.rationale: The event date (-10950, ~12,950 BP) sits almost exactly at the Younger Dryas onset, so the 'younger-dryas' row is the most appropriate detectability context (with some overlap into terminal upper-paleolithic). Ice sheets like Greenland's are exceptionally good preservation media for annually resolved chemical anomalies over ~13 millennia, and geological/sedimentary stratigraphy generally has high preservation odds this recently (geological=0.65), which matches the real-world fact that a platinum anomaly at this horizon has in fact been reported in Greenland ice (Petaev et al. 2013) and in numerous YDB sediment sites worldwide — i.e., this is not a purely speculative hypothesis but one with an actual, if contested, empirical literature. Astronomical detectability is nominally high (0.7) but is misleading here: it reflects general capacity to date orbital/impact-related celestial phenomena, not the ability to independently verify a 13,000-year-old fragmented-comet encounter, since no confirmed crater of the right age/size has been unambiguously matched (the Hiawatha crater's age is still debated and likely much older). Material (0.35), genetic (0.3), and iconographic/oral_tradition (0.1) evidence for a purely geophysical/atmospheric event are inherently weak categories — humans of this period left no writing, and any megafaunal or archaeological discontinuity is only weakly diagnostic of an impact specifically versus other Younger Dryas-onset climate mechanisms (e.g., meltwater pulse, AMOC shutdown). Overall, could_have_survived=true because ice-core and sediment stratigraphy realistically preserve chemical signals across this timespan, but the hypothesis remains empirically contested precisely because corroborating crater/astronomical evidence and unambiguous causal attribution (impact vs. terrestrial/volcanic/cosmic-dust sources) are still missing. A low score should not be used to explain away this absence, since geological/ice-core detectability is genuinely favorable in this period; the real epistemic gap is interpretive (causal mechanism), not preservational. I set the adjusted value slightly below the geological/astronomical ceiling (0.65/0.7) to reflect that the platinum-anomaly evidence itself is real-world documented but the specific 'impact-ejecta-fallout' causal mechanism (vs. alternative explanations for the anomaly) remains unconfirmed and debated.
